place.name: Family 266
place.aboutData: In this household each adult can consume goods and services worth about 685 US dollars each month. This consumption includes the things they buy as well as the things they produce for themselves (if any). We estimated this figure based on incomes reported by the family.
place.description:
The  family lives in Brazil. K is 24 years old and she works in telemarketing. Her brother M is 22 years old and he has a skilled job in production.

The family lives in their own 3 bedroom house and has been living here for 3 years. They like the size and location of the house. However, they dislike its lack of security. The house has uninterrupted electricity, indoors toilet facility, and safe supply of water.

The Family buys all of their food supplies from the market and spends around 30% of their income on it. They cook their food on LPG fuel. Drinking water is also available at their home and is safe to drink.

The family has been on vacations and has traveled as far as Vitoria, Brazil. Their favorite items in the house are the documents, mobile phones, TV, guitar etc. They are saving money and their next big plan is to buy a new TV and some living room furniture. Their dream is to buy a car.

currentTopic.description: A family’s stove type depends on income and access to clean fuels. The poorest, who are often in rural areas, use open charcoal or animal dung fires to heat a traditional or side-feed stove. Those with higher incomes use clean burning fuels like gas or electricity. The richest homes have integrated stoves and ovens that are safe, fan powered and have ready access to fuel.
currentTopic.name: Stove/hob

adding-spices-to-food-while-cooking.name_plural: Adding spices to food while cooking

bathrooms.description: The poorest families, particularly in rural areas, practice open defecation or use shallow pit latrines. Families with a higher income, especially in cities, have more access to improved sanitation facilities. Many middle income homes use ventilated outhouses with deep pits, protecting food and water sources from contamination. The richest families use integrated squat or seating toilets with a flush or septic tank to safely separate human excreta from human contact.
bathrooms.name: Bathroom/Toilet

beds.description: Materials, positioning and style of beds change across income levels. The poorest make do with natural fibres and unclean surfaces, while homes with more money sleep on raised platforms with purpose-made bedding for comfort. The richest homes often have more or less the same style mattresses, duvets and pillows, suggesting that there is globalized version of a comfortable night’s sleep.
beds.name: Bed

books.description: Families living on a very low income sometimes have poor literacy skills and often do not keep many books. Middle income families often have a big collection of children’s picture books and textbooks, which boosts children’s literacy rates. The richest families often borrow books from the library or buy novels to read for pleasure and so have a whole shelving unit allocated for books.
books.name: Books

computers.description: The poorest homes cannot afford computers or internet connections. Those with a higher income often have an affordable laptop or desktop connected to the internet through a cable. They might also use a smartphone connected to 3G data.  The richest homes often have high-tech computers complete with printing equipment and broadband internet.
computers.name: Computer

cooking-utensils.description: The cooking utensils a family has depends on economic level more than geographic region. The poorest families usually have one or two wooden spoons, metal serving spoons or sharp knives. Wealthier families have more materials to choose from, like colourful and heatproof plastics and stainless steel. The richest families have purpose made containers to display and organise their stash of various cooking utensils.
cooking-utensils.name: Cooking utensils

cups.description: Cups are functional and hold liquids that we drink, but also have a social use. The poorest around the world have just a small selection for drinking both hot and cold drinks. Those with a bit more money have special ceramic cups for hot and glass or metal cups for cold drinks. The richest families have diverse shapes, colours and materials on display in their kitchen cupboards or shelves.
cups.name: Cups/mugs/glasses

dish-brushes.description: The poorest families use rags made out of natural fibres or sometimes grit to wash plates. They do not tend to have manufactured materials or washing liquid. Those with more money use scrubbing brushes made of metal or plastic. The richest families use specially designed and colourful instruments to scrub plates clean. They have purpose made sinks or dishwasher machines.
dish-brushes.name: Dish washing brush/cloth

dish-racks.description: The poorest homes dry their small selection of metal or plastic dishes in a bowl or on the floor. Homes with a high income have a larger selection made out of different materials and leave dishes to dry in a purpose made drying space with bars allowing water to drain through. The richest homes sometimes have dishwashers.
dish-racks.name: Dish racks

families.description: Families all over the World are more similar than we might think. The poorest still get many children, but most families have about two children. Sometimes families take care of their elderly relatives as well as their children.
families.name: Family

floors.description: Those with the lowest income, especially in rural areas, make do with dirt or sand flooring which is hard to keep clean. Those with a higher income tend to have a tiled or plastic lino floor that is cheap to install and easy to maintain. The richest homes invest in ceramic or stone tiles and wooden floorboards to suit their preference.
floors.name: Floor

fruits.description: Fruit consumption is important to prevent chronic disease. Low income families can afford to eat only locally grown fruit when in season. Those with more money can also choose their preferred fruit from markets and shops. The richest can eat fruit imported from all over the world and store it in special fruit bowls or in their fridge.
fruits.name: Fruits and vegetables

get-water.description: Families living in rural poor communities often have to walk to water sources, and might lack clean drinking water. Middle income families tend to have improved water sources from taps which they might share with other families. They also tend to have a septic tank or filtering mechanism ensuring the water is clean. The richest homes have taps with reliable drinking water integrated into kitchens and bathrooms.
get-water.name: Get water

hand-washing.description: Hand washing after using the toilet is important for every family’s health. To do this, the poorest families collect water from wells or communal taps in plastic buckets or metal pots. Those with more money install an outdoor tap which can be used for hand washing. The richest have sinks with hot and cold taps installed inside their home which is easily accessible from the toilet.
hand-washing.name: Hand washing

how-the-most-loved-item-is-used.name: How the most loved item is used
how-the-most-loved-item-is-used.name_plural: How the most loved item is used

jewelry.description: Jewelry can be a life-saving insurance policy because it can be quickly exchanged for cash in a medical emergency. The poorest cannot afford any jewelry of value. For those with a higher income, jewelry is made from different materials like glass beads, gold and silver and is worn for pleasure. The richest often have jewelry boxes in their homes where they store many colorful necklaces, rings and earrings.
jewelry.name: Jewelry

light-sources.description: At night, the poorest homes have no light or any reliable light source, restricting how productive the family can be. Low to middle income homes use bare light bulbs to illuminate the home. The richest have diverse and personalised lighting in each room of their home, with sophisticated light dimmers and light shades.
light-sources.name: Light sources

lock-on-front-doors.description: The poorest families do not have locks and tend to make do with flimsy fibers to tie their doors shut. Middle income families often use cheap but effective padlocks on door frames to secure their homes. Finally, the richest use sophisticated integrated locks.
lock-on-front-doors.name: Lock on front door

meat.description: For the poorest, meat is a rare luxury and is consumed once every two to three months. Those with a higher income eat meat more regularly and keep it in fridges and freezers at home. They have also access to meat in food markets and shops. The richest families usually buy meat packaged and processed by food manufacturers.
meat.name: Meat or fish

medication.description: The variety and quality of medication that a family has available is dependent on income and the family’s local healthcare system. For the poorest, medication is devastatingly expensive so they have just a small supply. Those with a higher income have a variety, but the amount they can afford is dependent on state subsidies. The richest families keep many painkillers, preventative medicines and vitamin pills in cupboards or on shelves.
medication.name: Medication

most-loved-toys.description: Playing is important for early childhood development. The poorest families are not able to buy manufactured toys. Instead, children play with discarded objects in and outside the home. Wealthier families all over the world buy and make toys for their children, like footballs, wooden animals and teddy bears. The richest children also play with high-tech electronic games.
most-loved-toys.name: Most loved toy

next-big-things-i-plan-to-buy.name: Next big thing you are planning to buy
next-big-things-i-plan-to-buy.name_plural: Next big things I plan to buy

nicest-shoes.description: For the poorest, walking is the main mode of transport. Shoes are important to protect feet from diseases like hookworm and to help children get to school. Unfortunately, the poorest can seldom afford good shoes. With a little more money, the nicest shoes are often practical and good for long-distance walking. For the richer households, nicest shoes can be fashion accessories. Some have bright colors and high heels, not for long walks, but for leisure time.
nicest-shoes.name: Nicest shoes

papers.description: The use of paper changes according to income levels. Those with the lowest income might not read and write regularly, but often have a small amount of paper at home for children’s school work. Those with a higher income sometimes have ring bound notebooks or diaries to keep notes and dates in. The richest families also keep packs of white paper in their home for printing.
papers.name: Paper

pens.description: Not all low income families have pens at home, since they might not read and write regularly. Middle income families are usually highly literate, and mostly have some biro pens, colorful ballpoints or pencils kept inside a pencil case or pot because they are easy and cheap to buy. The richest families can buy all types of mass-manufactured pens and so usually have a large collection at home.
pens.name: Pen/pencils

phones.description: Most families in the World are connected by mobile phones, but phone functions vary according to income group. For the poorest families, mobile phones are usually for sending SMS messages. Middle income families sometimes have touch screen smartphones for sending images, videos and can be connected to internet services like online banking. In the richest households, the family members often have a phone each. Many of the richest homes use both smartphones and land lines.
phones.name: Phone

places-where-guests-are-served-dinner.name: Place where serving guests
places-where-guests-are-served-dinner.name_plural: Places where guests are served dinner

plates-of-food.description: The poorest survive on just one or two staple ingredients and availability varies according to season. They spend most of their income on food. Those with more money can eat food according to preference, nutritious value and taste, making meals using all food groups like dairy products, fruits and vegetables. The richest families can eat food imported from all over the world.
plates-of-food.name: Plate of food

play-areas.description: A safe place to play is important for children’s development. The poorest often do not have a safe outside space, making do with sometimes unsafe streets or fields. Families with more money allocate space for children to play like a playground with swings or an indoor space with toys. The richest families often have access to purpose-made climbing frames and sports fields nearby.
play-areas.name: Play area

plugging-into-and-out-of-power-outlet.name: Plugging into and out of power outlet
plugging-into-and-out-of-power-outlet.name_plural: Plugging into and out of power outlet

power-outlets.description: While many rural poor homes do not have electricity, many urban poor have unreliable access and power their homes using extension leads. Middle to high income families have integrated power outlets, although sometimes with loose wiring. The richest homes have safe and modern power outlets with wiring concealed in the walls.
power-outlets.name: Power outlet

power-switches.description: Electricity that can be controlled by switch is convenient and safe for families. The poorest make do with lighting kerosene lamps for light or making a fire for heat. Those with a higher income have loose power fittings without switches, risking dangerous electric shocks. The richest families have light and power switches incorporated into the walls of their home.
power-switches.name: Switch on/off

reading-a-book-seeing-the-back-of-book.name: Reading a book, seeing the back of book
reading-a-book-seeing-the-back-of-book.name_plural: Reading a book, seeing the back of book

reading-books-looking-over-the-shoulder.name: Reading a book, looking over the shoulder
reading-books-looking-over-the-shoulder.name_plural: Reading books, looking over the shoulder

roofs.description: All families need a roof over their head, but the materials available to the family depend on the economic level they live at. The poorest families use natural materials or cheap metal that struggles to withstand devastating weather, but can be packed up or replaced easily. The richest homes have sophisticated and durable roofs that are constructed by professional engineers.
roofs.name: Roof

salt.description: An essential part of every diet, most families store salt in their homes. In the poorest homes, families usually keep salt in brand-free plastic containers or pouches. Those with a higher income buy purpose made salt containers that have been packaged by food manufacturers. The richest families have a lot of different condiments to choose from and salt is placed in a designated space in the family’s kitchen.
salt.name: Salt

shaving.description: The poorest families use small blades or scissors to shave, while those with more disposable income buy purpose-made razors. Middle income families tend to buy the same style of razor everywhere in the world, usually temporary plastic ones.The richest families often have shaving foam, brushes and sometimes electric razors in their bathrooms.
shaving.name: Shaving

sitting-areas.description: A place to sit with friends and family is a central part of a home. The poorest sit on floors or rugs. Families with a higher income use wooden or plastic stools, chairs and tables to sit at and enjoy food and drinks together. The richest homes have more expensive furniture and decorate tables with tablecloths, and the chairs with fabric padding.
sitting-areas.name: Sitting area

soaps.description: Hand washing with soap reduces the risk of diarrhoeal disease, a leading cause of child mortality. The poorest families usually have a bar of soap to wash their hands with. Families with a higher income tend to buy soap in branded packages and keep it in a clean bucket or plastic box. The richest families buy liquid soap dispensers for hand washing, choosing from many fragrances and colours.
soaps.name: Soap for hands and body

social-drinks.description: Drinks that families enjoy together vary more across income level than they do location. The poorest families prize clean water highly, and those with some spare money heat it up with tea or coffee. Wealthier families buy juice, alcoholic and fizzy drinks. The richest homes buy manufactured tea bags and coffee machines for convenience, a luxury poorer homes cannot afford.
social-drinks.name: Social drink

steam-exits.description: A chimney or steam exit prevents household air pollution. For the poorest, solid fuels like animal dung or charcoal are often burnt for cooking and heating. These fuels produce hazardous fumes like carbon monoxide. To prevent the buildup of smoke over stoves, the poorest have gaps in the roofing, while wealthier homes have purpose-made ventilation. The richest use electronic steam extractors over their stoves.
steam-exits.name: Smoke and steam exit

The poorest, who are often in rural areas, use open charcoal or animal dung fires to heat a traditional or side-feed stove. Those with higher incomes use clean burning fuels like gas or electricity. The richest homes have integrated stoves and ovens that are safe, fan powered and have ready access to fuel.
stoves.name: Stove/hob

tables-with-food.name: Table with food

things-i-dream-of-having.description: The poorest families dream of getting out of poverty and having a bicycle, piece of land or a better house. Families who do not live under the poverty line dream of affluence and education. Middle income families wish for a university education and having a big house. The richest families dream of flying to new places and buying cars.
things-i-dream-of-having.name: Thing I dream about having

toilet-paper.description: The poorest families use water or leaves to clean themselves after the toilet. With more money families might start using toilet paper. The richest families use a roll of toilet paper. They also have a special brush and washing liquid to clean the toilet with.
toilet-paper.name: Toilet paper

toothbrushes.description: The poorest homes do not have toothbrushes, but use twigs and sand as toothpick tools instead. Families with a slightly higher income buy a plastic toothbrush to share since they cannot afford one each. The richest homes often buy special teeth cleaning products like flavored toothpaste, mouthwash or an electric toothbrush.
toothbrushes.name: Toothbrush

The richest children also play with high-tech electronic games.
toys.name: Toys

vegetables.description: Vegetable consumption is important to prevent against chronic disease. Low income families eat locally grown produce, and usually just have a couple to choose from at any one time. Those with more money can choose their preferred type from markets and shops. The richest eat their favourite vegetables imported from all over the world and store them in their fridge or in purpose made vegetable containers.
vegetables.name: Vegetables

washing-clothes.description: The poorest usually wash their clothes in open water or a bucket, without specialised washing liquid. Middle income families often have a tap supplying running water. The richest families use washing, and sometimes drying, machines to clean their clothes.
washing-clothes.name: Washing clothes/cleaning

what-i-wish-i-could-buy.name: What I wish I could buy
what-i-wish-i-could-buy.name_plural: What I wish I could buy

Those with a higher income sometimes install a desk to work or study at along with a comfortable chair. The richest homes have more disposable income to spend on work areas with desk lamps, computers and printing equipment.

most-loved-toys.name: Most loved toy

next-big-things-i-plan-to-buy.name: Next big thing you are planning to buy

nicest-shoes.description: For the poorest, walking is the main mode of transport. Shoes are important to protect feet from diseases like hookworm and to help children get to school. Unfortunately, the poorest can seldom afford good shoes. With a little more money, the nicest shoes are often practical and good for long-distance walking. For the richer households, nicest shoes can be fashion accessories. Some have bright colors and high heels, not for long walks, but for leisure time.
nicest-shoes.name: Nicest shoes

papers.description: The use of paper changes according to income levels. Those with the lowest income might not read and write regularly, but often have a small amount of paper at home for children’s school work. Those with a higher income sometimes have ring bound notebooks or diaries to keep notes and dates in. The richest families also keep packs of white paper in their home for printing.
papers.name: Paper

pens.description: Not all low income families have pens at home, since they might not read and write regularly. Middle income families are usually highly literate, and mostly have some biro pens, colorful ballpoints or pencils kept inside a pencil case or pot because they are easy and cheap to buy. The richest families can buy all types of mass-manufactured pens and so usually have a large collection at home.
pens.name: Pen/pencils

phones.description: Most families in the World are connected by mobile phones, but phone functions vary according to income group. For the poorest families, mobile phones are usually for sending SMS messages. Middle income families sometimes have touch screen smartphones for sending images, videos and can be connected to internet services like online banking. In the richest households, the family members often have a phone each. Many of the richest homes use both smartphones and land lines.
phones.name: Phone

places-where-guests-are-served-dinner.name: Place where serving guests
places-where-guests-are-served-dinner.name_plural: Places where guests are served dinner

plates-of-food.description: The poorest survive on just one or two staple ingredients and availability varies according to season. They spend most of their income on food. Those with more money can eat food according to preference, nutritious value and taste, making meals using all food groups like dairy products, fruits and vegetables. The richest families can eat food imported from all over the world.
plates-of-food.name: Plate of food

play-areas.description: A safe place to play is important for children’s development. The poorest often do not have a safe outside space, making do with sometimes unsafe streets or fields. Families with more money allocate space for children to play like a playground with swings or an indoor space with toys. The richest families often have access to purpose-made climbing frames and sports fields nearby.
play-areas.name: Play area

plugging-into-and-out-of-power-outlet.name: Plugging into and out of power outlet
plugging-into-and-out-of-power-outlet.name_plural: Plugging into and out of power outlet

power-outlets.description: While many rural poor homes do not have electricity, many urban poor have unreliable access and power their homes using extension leads. Middle to high income families have integrated power outlets, although sometimes with loose wiring. The richest homes have safe and modern power outlets with wiring concealed in the walls.
power-outlets.name: Power outlet

power-switches.description: Electricity that can be controlled by switch is convenient and safe for families. The poorest make do with lighting kerosene lamps for light or making a fire for heat. power-switches.name: Switch on/off

reading-a-book-seeing-the-back-of-book.name: Reading a book, seeing the back of book

reading-books-looking-over-the-shoulder.name: Reading a book, looking over the shoulder

roofs.description: All families need a roof over their head, but the materials available to the family depend on the economic level they live at. The poorest families use natural materials or cheap metal that struggles to withstand devastating weather, but can be packed up or replaced easily. The richest homes have sophisticated and durable roofs that are constructed by professional engineers.
roofs.name: Roof

salt.description: An essential part of every diet, most families store salt in their homes. In the poorest homes, families usually keep salt in brand-free plastic containers or pouches. Those with a higher income buy purpose made salt containers that have been packaged by food manufacturers. The richest families have a lot of different condiments to choose from and salt is placed in a designated space in the family’s kitchen.
salt.name: Salt

shaving.description: The poorest families use small blades or scissors to shave, while those with more disposable income buy purpose-made razors. Middle income families tend to buy the same style of razor everywhere in the world, usually temporary plastic ones.The richest families often have shaving foam, brushes and sometimes electric razors in their bathrooms.
shaving.name: Shaving

sitting-areas.description: A place to sit with friends and family is a central part of a home. The poorest sit on floors or rugs. Families with a higher income use wooden or plastic stools, chairs and tables to sit at and enjoy food and drinks together. The richest homes have more expensive furniture and decorate tables with tablecloths, and the chairs with fabric padding.
sitting-areas.name: Sitting area

soaps.description: Hand washing with soap reduces the risk of diarrhoeal disease, a leading cause of child mortality. The poorest families usually have a bar of soap to wash their hands with. Families with a higher income tend to buy soap in branded packages and keep it in a clean bucket or plastic box. The richest families buy liquid soap dispensers for hand washing, choosing from many fragrances and colours.
soaps.name: Soap for hands and body

social-drinks.description: Drinks that families enjoy together vary more across income level than they do location. The poorest families prize clean water highly, and those with some spare money heat it up with tea or coffee. Wealthier families buy juice, alcoholic and fizzy drinks. The richest homes buy manufactured tea bags and coffee machines for convenience, a luxury poorer homes cannot afford.
social-drinks.name: Social drink

These fuels produce hazardous fumes like carbon monoxide. To prevent the buildup of smoke over stoves, the poorest have gaps in the roofing, while wealthier homes have purpose-made ventilation. The richest use electronic steam extractors over their stoves.
steam-exits.name: Smoke and steam exit

stoves.description: A family’s stove type depends on income and access to clean fuels. The poorest, who are often in rural areas, use open charcoal or animal dung fires to heat a traditional or side-feed stove. Those with higher incomes use clean burning fuels like gas or electricity. The richest homes have integrated stoves and ovens that are safe, fan powered and have ready access to fuel.
stoves.name: Stove/hob

tables-with-food.name: Table with food

The richest families dream of flying to new places and buying cars.
things-i-dream-of-having.name: Thing I dream about having

toilet-paper.description: The poorest families use water or leaves to clean themselves after the toilet. With more money families might start using toilet paper. The richest families use a roll of toilet paper. They also have a special brush and washing liquid to clean the toilet with.
toilet-paper.name: Toilet paper

toilets.description: The poorest families, particularly in rural areas, practice open defecation or use shallow pit latrines. Families with a higher income, especially in cities, have more access to improved sanitation facilities. Many middle income homes use ventilated outhouses with deep pits, protecting food and water sources from contamination. The richest families use integrated squat or seating toilets with a flush or septic tank to safely separate human excreta from human contact.
toilets.name: Toilet

toothbrushes.description: The poorest homes do not have toothbrushes, but use twigs and sand as toothpick tools instead. Families with a slightly higher income buy a plastic toothbrush to share since they cannot afford one each. The richest homes often buy special teeth cleaning products like flavored toothpaste, mouthwash or an electric toothbrush.
toothbrushes.name: Toothbrush

toys.description: Playing is important for early childhood development. The poorest families are not able to buy manufactured toys. toys.name: Toys

vegetables.description: Vegetable consumption is important to prevent against chronic disease. Low income families eat locally grown produce, and usually just have a couple to choose from at any one time. Those with more money can choose their preferred type from markets and shops. The richest eat their favourite vegetables imported from all over the world and store them in their fridge or in purpose made vegetable containers.
vegetables.name: Vegetables

washing-clothes.description: The poorest usually wash their clothes in open water or a bucket, without specialised washing liquid. Middle income families often have a tap supplying running water. The richest families use washing, and sometimes drying, machines to clean their clothes.
washing-clothes.name: Washing clothes/cleaning

what-i-wish-i-could-buy.name: What I wish I could buy
what-i-wish-i-could-buy.name_plural: What I wish I could buy

work-areas.description: The poorest families work areas all look different and are often outside, since they often do physical work like rickshaw driving, sewing or farming. Those with a higher income sometimes install a desk to work or study at along with a comfortable chair. The richest homes have more disposable income to spend on work areas with desk lamps, computers and printing equipment.
work-areas.name: Work area

The poorest make do with natural fibres and unclean surfaces, while homes with more money sleep on raised platforms with purpose-made bedding for comfort. beds.name: Bed

computers.description: The poorest homes cannot afford computers or internet connections. The richest homes often have high-tech computers complete with printing equipment and broadband internet.
computers.name: Computer

cooking-utensils.description: The cooking utensils a family has depends on economic level more than geographic region. The poorest families usually have one or two wooden spoons, metal serving spoons or sharp knives. Wealthier families have more materials to choose from, like colourful and heatproof plastics and stainless steel. The richest families have purpose made containers to display and organise their stash of various cooking utensils.
cooking-utensils.name: Cooking utensils

cups.description: Cups are functional and hold liquids that we drink, but also have a social use. The poorest around the world have just a small selection for drinking both hot and cold drinks. Those with a bit more money have special ceramic cups for hot and glass or metal cups for cold drinks. The richest families have diverse shapes, colours and materials on display in their kitchen cupboards or shelves.
cups.name: Cups/mugs/glasses

dish-brushes.description: The poorest families use rags made out of natural fibres or sometimes grit to wash plates. They do not tend to have manufactured materials or washing liquid. Those with more money use scrubbing brushes made of metal or plastic. The richest families use specially designed and colourful instruments to scrub plates clean. They have purpose made sinks or dishwasher machines.
dish-brushes.name: Dish washing brush/cloth

dish-racks.description: The poorest homes dry their small selection of metal or plastic dishes in a bowl or on the floor. Homes with a high income have a larger selection made out of different materials and leave dishes to dry in a purpose made drying space with bars allowing water to drain through. The richest homes sometimes have dishwashers.
dish-racks.name: Dish racks

families.name: Family

floors.name: Floor

fruits.description: Fruit consumption is important to prevent chronic disease. Low income families can afford to eat only locally grown fruit when in season. Those with more money can also choose their preferred fruit from markets and shops. The richest can eat fruit imported from all over the world and store it in special fruit bowls or in their fridge.
fruits.name: Fruits and vegetables

get-water.description: Families living in rural poor communities often have to walk to water sources, and might lack clean drinking water. Middle income families tend to have improved water sources from taps which they might share with other families. They also tend to have a septic tank or filtering mechanism ensuring the water is clean. The richest homes have taps with reliable drinking water integrated into kitchens and bathrooms.
get-water.name: Get water

hand-washing.description: Hand washing after using the toilet is important for every family’s health. To do this, the poorest families collect water from wells or communal taps in plastic buckets or metal pots. Those with more money install an outdoor tap which can be used for hand washing. The richest have sinks with hot and cold taps installed inside their home which is easily accessible from the toilet.
hand-washing.name: Hand washing

how-the-most-loved-item-is-used.name: How the most loved item is used
how-the-most-loved-item-is-used.name_plural: How the most loved item is used

jewelry.description: Jewelry can be a life-saving insurance policy because it can be quickly exchanged for cash in a medical emergency. The poorest cannot afford any jewelry of value. For those with a higher income, jewelry is made from different materials like glass beads, gold and silver and is worn for pleasure. The richest often have jewelry boxes in their homes where they store many colorful necklaces, rings and earrings.
jewelry.name: Jewelry

light-sources.description: At night, the poorest homes have no light or any reliable light source, restricting how productive the family can be. Low to middle income homes use bare light bulbs to illuminate the home. The richest have diverse and personalised lighting in each room of their home, with sophisticated light dimmers and light shades.
light-sources.name: Light sources

lock-on-front-doors.description: The poorest families do not have locks and tend to make do with flimsy fibers to tie their doors shut. Middle income families often use cheap but effective padlocks on door frames to secure their homes. Finally, the richest use sophisticated integrated locks.
lock-on-front-doors.name: Lock on front door

meat.description: For the poorest, meat is a rare luxury and is consumed once every two to three months. Those with a higher income eat meat more regularly and keep it in fridges and freezers at home. They have also access to meat in food markets and shops. The richest families usually buy meat packaged and processed by food manufacturers.
meat.name: Meat or fish

For the poorest, medication is devastatingly expensive so they have just a small supply. Those with a higher income have a variety, but the amount they can afford is dependent on state subsidies. The richest families keep many painkillers, preventative medicines and vitamin pills in cupboards or on shelves.
medication.name: Medication

Low income families eat locally grown produce, and usually just have a couple to choose from at any one time. Those with more money can choose their preferred type from markets and shops. The richest eat their favourite vegetables imported from all over the world and store them in their fridge or in purpose made vegetable containers.
vegetables.name: Vegetables

washing-clothes.description: The poorest usually wash their clothes in open water or a bucket, without specialised washing liquid. Middle income families often have a tap supplying running water. The richest families use washing, and sometimes drying, machines to clean their clothes.
washing-clothes.name: Washing clothes/cleaning

what-i-wish-i-could-buy.name: What I wish I could buy
what-i-wish-i-could-buy.name_plural: What I wish I could buy

work-areas.description: The poorest families work areas all look different and are often outside, since they often do physical work like rickshaw driving, sewing or farming. Those with a higher income sometimes install a desk to work or study at along with a comfortable chair. The richest homes have more disposable income to spend on work areas with desk lamps, computers and printing equipment.
work-areas.name: Work area

beds.description: Materials, positioning and style of beds change across income levels. The poorest make do with natural fibres and unclean surfaces, while homes with more money sleep on raised platforms with purpose-made bedding for comfort. The richest homes often have more or less the same style mattresses, duvets and pillows, suggesting that there is globalized version of a comfortable night’s sleep.
beds.name: Bed

families.description: Families all over the World are more similar than we might think. The poorest still get many children, but most families have about two children. Sometimes families take care of their elderly relatives as well as their children.
families.name: Family

floors.description: Those with the lowest income, especially in rural areas, make do with dirt or sand flooring which is hard to keep clean. Those with a higher income tend to have a tiled or plastic lino floor that is cheap to install and easy to maintain. The richest homes invest in ceramic or stone tiles and wooden floorboards to suit their preference.
floors.name: Floor

stoves.description: A family’s stove type depends on income and access to clean fuels. The poorest, who are often in rural areas, use open charcoal or animal dung fires to heat a traditional or side-feed stove. Those with higher incomes use clean burning fuels like gas or electricity. The richest homes have integrated stoves and ovens that are safe, fan powered and have ready access to fuel.
stoves.name: Stove/hob

toilets.description: The poorest families, particularly in rural areas, practice open defecation or use shallow pit latrines. Families with a higher income, especially in cities, have more access to improved sanitation facilities. Many middle income homes use ventilated outhouses with deep pits, protecting food and water sources from contamination. The richest families use integrated squat or seating toilets with a flush or septic tank to safely separate human excreta from human contact.
toilets.name: Toilet

toothbrushes.description: The poorest homes do not have toothbrushes, but use twigs and sand as toothpick tools instead. Families with a slightly higher income buy a plastic toothbrush to share since they cannot afford one each. The richest homes often buy special teeth cleaning products like flavored toothpaste, mouthwash or an electric toothbrush.
toothbrushes.name: Toothbrush

toys.description: Playing is important for early childhood development. The poorest families are not able to buy manufactured toys. Instead, children play with discarded objects in and outside the home. Wealthier families all over the world buy and make toys for their children, like footballs, wooden animals and teddy bears. The richest children also play with high-tech electronic games.
toys.name: Toys

adding-spices-to-food-while-cooking.name: Adding spices to food while cooking
adding-spices-to-food-while-cooking.name_plural: Adding spices to food while cooking

bathrooms.description: The poorest families, particularly in rural areas, practice open defecation or use shallow pit latrines. books.description: Families living on a very low income sometimes have poor literacy skills and often do not keep many books. Middle income families often have a big collection of children’s picture books and textbooks, which boosts children’s literacy rates. The richest families often borrow books from the library or buy novels to read for pleasure and so have a whole shelving unit allocated for books.
books.name: Books

computers.description: The poorest homes cannot afford computers or internet connections. Those with a higher income often have an affordable laptop or desktop connected to the internet through a cable. They might also use a smartphone connected to 3G data.  The richest homes often have high-tech computers complete with printing equipment and broadband internet.
computers.name: Computer

cooking-utensils.description: The cooking utensils a family has depends on economic level more than geographic region. The poorest families usually have one or two wooden spoons, metal serving spoons or sharp knives. Wealthier families have more materials to choose from, like colourful and heatproof plastics and stainless steel. The richest families have purpose made containers to display and organise their stash of various cooking utensils.
cooking-utensils.name: Cooking utensils

cups.description: Cups are functional and hold liquids that we drink, but also have a social use. The poorest around the world have just a small selection for drinking both hot and cold drinks. Those with a bit more money have special ceramic cups for hot and glass or metal cups for cold drinks. The richest families have diverse shapes, colours and materials on display in their kitchen cupboards or shelves.
cups.name: Cups/mugs/glasses

dish-brushes.description: The poorest families use rags made out of natural fibres or sometimes grit to wash plates. They do not tend to have manufactured materials or washing liquid. Those with more money use scrubbing brushes made of metal or plastic. The richest families use specially designed and colourful instruments to scrub plates clean. They have purpose made sinks or dishwasher machines.
dish-brushes.name: Dish washing brush/cloth

dish-racks.description: The poorest homes dry their small selection of metal or plastic dishes in a bowl or on the floor. Homes with a high income have a larger selection made out of different materials and leave dishes to dry in a purpose made drying space with bars allowing water to drain through. The richest homes sometimes have dishwashers.
dish-racks.name: Dish racks

families.description: Families all over the World are more similar than we might think. The poorest still get many children, but most families have about two children. Sometimes families take care of their elderly relatives as well as their children.
families.name: Family

Those with a higher income tend to have a tiled or plastic lino floor that is cheap to install and easy to maintain. The richest homes invest in ceramic or stone tiles and wooden floorboards to suit their preference.
floors.name: Floor

fruits.description: Fruit consumption is important to prevent chronic disease. Low income families can afford to eat only locally grown fruit when in season. Those with more money can also choose their preferred fruit from markets and shops. The richest can eat fruit imported from all over the world and store it in special fruit bowls or in their fridge.
fruits.name: Fruits and vegetables

get-water.description: Families living in rural poor communities often have to walk to water sources, and might lack clean drinking water. Middle income families tend to have improved water sources from taps which they might share with other families. They also tend to have a septic tank or filtering mechanism ensuring the water is clean. The richest homes have taps with reliable drinking water integrated into kitchens and bathrooms.
get-water.name: Get water

hand-washing.description: Hand washing after using the toilet is important for every family’s health. To do this, the poorest families collect water from wells or communal taps in plastic buckets or metal pots. Those with more money install an outdoor tap which can be used for hand washing. The richest have sinks with hot and cold taps installed inside their home which is easily accessible from the toilet.
hand-washing.name: Hand washing

how-the-most-loved-item-is-used.name: How the most loved item is used
how-the-most-loved-item-is-used.name_plural: How the most loved item is used

jewelry.description: Jewelry can be a life-saving insurance policy because it can be quickly exchanged for cash in a medical emergency. The poorest cannot afford any jewelry of value. For those with a higher income, jewelry is made from different materials like glass beads, gold and silver and is worn for pleasure. The richest often have jewelry boxes in their homes where they store many colorful necklaces, rings and earrings.
jewelry.name: Jewelry

light-sources.description: At night, the poorest homes have no light or any reliable light source, restricting how productive the family can be. Low to middle income homes use bare light bulbs to illuminate the home. The richest have diverse and personalised lighting in each room of their home, with sophisticated light dimmers and light shades.
light-sources.name: Light sources

light-sources-in-livingroom.description: At night, the poorest homes have no light or any reliable light source, restricting how productive the family can be. light-sources-in-livingroom.name: Light source in livingroom

light-sources-kitchen.name: Light source in kitchen

lightsources-by-bed-reading-light.description: At night, the poorest homes have no light or any reliable light source, restricting how productive the family can be. The richest have diverse and personalised lighting in each room of their home, with sophisticated light dimmers and light shades.
lightsources-by-bed-reading-light.name: Lightsources by bed, reading light

lock-on-front-doors.description: The poorest families do not have locks and tend to make do with flimsy fibers to tie their doors shut. Middle income families often use cheap but effective padlocks on door frames to secure their homes. Finally, the richest use sophisticated integrated locks.
lock-on-front-doors.name: Lock on front door

meat.description: For the poorest, meat is a rare luxury and is consumed once every two to three months. Those with a higher income eat meat more regularly and keep it in fridges and freezers at home. They have also access to meat in food markets and shops. The richest families usually buy meat packaged and processed by food manufacturers.
meat.name: Meat or fish

medication.description: The variety and quality of medication that a family has available is dependent on income and the family’s local healthcare system. For the poorest, medication is devastatingly expensive so they have just a small supply. Those with a higher income have a variety, but the amount they can afford is dependent on state subsidies. The richest families keep many painkillers, preventative medicines and vitamin pills in cupboards or on shelves.
medication.name: Medication

most-loved-toys.description: Playing is important for early childhood development. The poorest families are not able to buy manufactured toys. Instead, children play with discarded objects in and outside the home. Wealthier families all over the world buy and make toys for their children, like footballs, wooden animals and teddy bears. The richest children also play with high-tech electronic games.
most-loved-toys.name: Most loved toy

next-big-things-i-plan-to-buy.name: Next big thing you are planning to buy
next-big-things-i-plan-to-buy.name_plural: Next big things I plan to buy

nicest-shoes.description: For the poorest, walking is the main mode of transport. Shoes are important to protect feet from diseases like hookworm and to help children get to school. Unfortunately, the poorest can seldom afford good shoes. With a little more money, the nicest shoes are often practical and good for long-distance walking. For the richer households, nicest shoes can be fashion accessories. Some have bright colors and high heels, not for long walks, but for leisure time.
nicest-shoes.name: Nicest shoes

papers.description: The use of paper changes according to income levels. Those with the lowest income might not read and write regularly, but often have a small amount of paper at home for children’s school work. Those with a higher income sometimes have ring bound notebooks or diaries to keep notes and dates in. The richest families also keep packs of white paper in their home for printing.
papers.name: Paper

pens.description: Not all low income families have pens at home, since they might not read and write regularly. Middle income families are usually highly literate, and mostly have some biro pens, colorful ballpoints or pencils kept inside a pencil case or pot because they are easy and cheap to buy. The richest families can buy all types of mass-manufactured pens and so usually have a large collection at home.
pens.name: Pen/pencils

phones.description: Most families in the World are connected by mobile phones, but phone functions vary according to income group. For the poorest families, mobile phones are usually for sending SMS messages. Middle income families sometimes have touch screen smartphones for sending images, videos and can be connected to internet services like online banking. In the richest households, the family members often have a phone each. Many of the richest homes use both smartphones and land lines.
phones.name: Phone

places-where-guests-are-served-dinner.name: Place where serving guests
places-where-guests-are-served-dinner.name_plural: Places where guests are served dinner

plates-of-food.description: The poorest survive on just one or two staple ingredients and availability varies according to season. They spend most of their income on food. Those with more money can eat food according to preference, nutritious value and taste, making meals using all food groups like dairy products, fruits and vegetables. The richest families can eat food imported from all over the world.
plates-of-food.name: Plate of food

play-areas.description: A safe place to play is important for children’s development. The poorest often do not have a safe outside space, making do with sometimes unsafe streets or fields. Families with more money allocate space for children to play like a playground with swings or an indoor space with toys. The richest families often have access to purpose-made climbing frames and sports fields nearby.
play-areas.name: Play area

plugging-into-and-out-of-power-outlet.name: Plugging into and out of power outlet
plugging-into-and-out-of-power-outlet.name_plural: Plugging into and out of power outlet

power-outlets.description: While many rural poor homes do not have electricity, many urban poor have unreliable access and power their homes using extension leads. Middle to high income families have integrated power outlets, although sometimes with loose wiring. The richest homes have safe and modern power outlets with wiring concealed in the walls.
power-outlets.name: Power outlet

power-switches.description: Electricity that can be controlled by switch is convenient and safe for families. The poorest make do with lighting kerosene lamps for light or making a fire for heat. Those with a higher income have loose power fittings without switches, risking dangerous electric shocks. The richest families have light and power switches incorporated into the walls of their home.
power-switches.name: Switch on/off

reading-a-book-seeing-the-back-of-book.name: Reading a book, seeing the back of book
reading-a-book-seeing-the-back-of-book.name_plural: Reading a book, seeing the back of book

reading-books-looking-over-the-shoulder.name: Reading a book, looking over the shoulder
reading-books-looking-over-the-shoulder.name_plural: Reading books, looking over the shoulder

roofs.description: All families need a roof over their head, but the materials available to the family depend on the economic level they live at. The poorest families use natural materials or cheap metal that struggles to withstand devastating weather, but can be packed up or replaced easily. The richest homes have sophisticated and durable roofs that are constructed by professional engineers.
roofs.name: Roof

salt.description: An essential part of every diet, most families store salt in their homes. In the poorest homes, families usually keep salt in brand-free plastic containers or pouches. Those with a higher income buy purpose made salt containers that have been packaged by food manufacturers. The richest families have a lot of different condiments to choose from and salt is placed in a designated space in the family’s kitchen.
salt.name: Salt

shaving.description: The poorest families use small blades or scissors to shave, while those with more disposable income buy purpose-made razors. Middle income families tend to buy the same style of razor everywhere in the world, usually temporary plastic ones.The richest families often have shaving foam, brushes and sometimes electric razors in their bathrooms.
shaving.name: Shaving

sitting-areas.description: A place to sit with friends and family is a central part of a home. The poorest sit on floors or rugs. Families with a higher income use wooden or plastic stools, chairs and tables to sit at and enjoy food and drinks together. The richest homes have more expensive furniture and decorate tables with tablecloths, and the chairs with fabric padding.
sitting-areas.name: Sitting area

soaps.description: Hand washing with soap reduces the risk of diarrhoeal disease, a leading cause of child mortality. The poorest families usually have a bar of soap to wash their hands with. Families with a higher income tend to buy soap in branded packages and keep it in a clean bucket or plastic box. The richest families buy liquid soap dispensers for hand washing, choosing from many fragrances and colours.
soaps.name: Soap for hands and body

social-drinks.description: Drinks that families enjoy together vary more across income level than they do location. The poorest families prize clean water highly, and those with some spare money heat it up with tea or coffee. Wealthier families buy juice, alcoholic and fizzy drinks. The richest homes buy manufactured tea bags and coffee machines for convenience, a luxury poorer homes cannot afford.
social-drinks.name: Social drink

steam-exits.description: A chimney or steam exit prevents household air pollution. For the poorest, solid fuels like animal dung or charcoal are often burnt for cooking and heating. These fuels produce hazardous fumes like carbon monoxide. To prevent the buildup of smoke over stoves, the poorest have gaps in the roofing, while wealthier homes have purpose-made ventilation. The richest use electronic steam extractors over their stoves.
steam-exits.name: Smoke and steam exit

things-i-dream-of-having.description: The poorest families dream of getting out of poverty and having a bicycle, piece of land or a better house. Families who do not live under the poverty line dream of affluence and education. Middle income families wish for a university education and having a big house. The richest families dream of flying to new places and buying cars.
things-i-dream-of-having.name: Thing I dream about having

toilet-paper.description: The poorest families use water or leaves to clean themselves after the toilet. With more money families might start using toilet paper. The richest families use a roll of toilet paper. They also have a special brush and washing liquid to clean the toilet with.
toilet-paper.name: Toilet paper

Low to middle income homes use bare light bulbs to illuminate the home. The richest have diverse and personalised lighting in each room of their home, with sophisticated light dimmers and light shades.
light-sources-kitchen.name: Light source in kitchen

lightsources-by-bed-reading-light.description: At night, the poorest homes have no light or any reliable light source, restricting how productive the family can be. Low to middle income homes use bare light bulbs to illuminate the home. The richest have diverse and personalised lighting in each room of their home, with sophisticated light dimmers and light shades.
lightsources-by-bed-reading-light.name: Lightsources by bed, reading light

lock-on-front-doors.description: The poorest families do not have locks and tend to make do with flimsy fibers to tie their doors shut. Middle income families often use cheap but effective padlocks on door frames to secure their homes. Finally, the richest use sophisticated integrated locks.
lock-on-front-doors.name: Lock on front door

meat.description: For the poorest, meat is a rare luxury and is consumed once every two to three months. Those with a higher income eat meat more regularly and keep it in fridges and freezers at home. They have also access to meat in food markets and shops. The richest families usually buy meat packaged and processed by food manufacturers.
meat.name: Meat or fish

medication.description: The variety and quality of medication that a family has available is dependent on income and the family’s local healthcare system. For the poorest, medication is devastatingly expensive so they have just a small supply. Those with a higher income have a variety, but the amount they can afford is dependent on state subsidies. The richest families keep many painkillers, preventative medicines and vitamin pills in cupboards or on shelves.
medication.name: Medication

most-loved-toys.description: Playing is important for early childhood development. The poorest families are not able to buy manufactured toys. Instead, children play with discarded objects in and outside the home. Wealthier families all over the world buy and make toys for their children, like footballs, wooden animals and teddy bears. The richest children also play with high-tech electronic games.
most-loved-toys.name: Most loved toy

next-big-things-i-plan-to-buy.name: Next big thing you are planning to buy
next-big-things-i-plan-to-buy.name_plural: Next big things I plan to buy

nicest-shoes.description: For the poorest, walking is the main mode of transport. Shoes are important to protect feet from diseases like hookworm and to help children get to school. Unfortunately, the poorest can seldom afford good shoes. With a little more money, the nicest shoes are often practical and good for long-distance walking. For the richer households, nicest shoes can be fashion accessories. Some have bright colors and high heels, not for long walks, but for leisure time.
nicest-shoes.name: Nicest shoes

papers.description: The use of paper changes according to income levels. Those with the lowest income might not read and write regularly, but often have a small amount of paper at home for children’s school work. Those with a higher income sometimes have ring bound notebooks or diaries to keep notes and dates in. The richest families also keep packs of white paper in their home for printing.
papers.name: Paper

pens.description: Not all low income families have pens at home, since they might not read and write regularly. Middle income families are usually highly literate, and mostly have some biro pens, colorful ballpoints or pencils kept inside a pencil case or pot because they are easy and cheap to buy. The richest families can buy all types of mass-manufactured pens and so usually have a large collection at home.
pens.name: Pen/pencils

phones.description: Most families in the World are connected by mobile phones, but phone functions vary according to income group. For the poorest families, mobile phones are usually for sending SMS messages. Middle income families sometimes have touch screen smartphones for sending images, videos and can be connected to internet services like online banking. In the richest households, the family members often have a phone each. Many of the richest homes use both smartphones and land lines.
phones.name: Phone

places-where-guests-are-served-dinner.name: Place where serving guests
places-where-guests-are-served-dinner.name_plural: Places where guests are served dinner

plates-of-food.description: The poorest survive on just one or two staple ingredients and availability varies according to season. They spend most of their income on food. Those with more money can eat food according to preference, nutritious value and taste, making meals using all food groups like dairy products, fruits and vegetables. The richest families can eat food imported from all over the world.
plates-of-food.name: Plate of food

play-areas.description: A safe place to play is important for children’s development. The poorest often do not have a safe outside space, making do with sometimes unsafe streets or fields. Families with more money allocate space for children to play like a playground with swings or an indoor space with toys. The richest families often have access to purpose-made climbing frames and sports fields nearby.
play-areas.name: Play area

plugging-into-and-out-of-power-outlet.name: Plugging into and out of power outlet
plugging-into-and-out-of-power-outlet.name_plural: Plugging into and out of power outlet

power-outlets.description: While many rural poor homes do not have electricity, many urban poor have unreliable access and power their homes using extension leads. Middle to high income families have integrated power outlets, although sometimes with loose wiring. The richest homes have safe and modern power outlets with wiring concealed in the walls.
power-outlets.name: Power outlet

power-switches.description: Electricity that can be controlled by switch is convenient and safe for families. The poorest make do with lighting kerosene lamps for light or making a fire for heat. Those with a higher income have loose power fittings without switches, risking dangerous electric shocks. The richest families have light and power switches incorporated into the walls of their home.
power-switches.name: Switch on/off

reading-a-book-seeing-the-back-of-book.name: Reading a book, seeing the back of book
reading-a-book-seeing-the-back-of-book.name_plural: Reading a book, seeing the back of book

reading-books-looking-over-the-shoulder.name: Reading a book, looking over the shoulder
reading-books-looking-over-the-shoulder.name_plural: Reading books, looking over the shoulder

roofs.description: All families need a roof over their head, but the materials available to the family depend on the economic level they live at. The poorest families use natural materials or cheap metal that struggles to withstand devastating weather, but can be packed up or replaced easily. The richest homes have sophisticated and durable roofs that are constructed by professional engineers.
roofs.name: Roof

salt.description: An essential part of every diet, most families store salt in their homes. In the poorest homes, families usually keep salt in brand-free plastic containers or pouches. Those with a higher income buy purpose made salt containers that have been packaged by food manufacturers. The richest families have a lot of different condiments to choose from and salt is placed in a designated space in the family’s kitchen.
salt.name: Salt

shaving.description: The poorest families use small blades or scissors to shave, while those with more disposable income buy purpose-made razors. Middle income families tend to buy the same style of razor everywhere in the world, usually temporary plastic ones.The richest families often have shaving foam, brushes and sometimes electric razors in their bathrooms.
shaving.name: Shaving

sitting-areas.description: A place to sit with friends and family is a central part of a home. The poorest sit on floors or rugs. Families with a higher income use wooden or plastic stools, chairs and tables to sit at and enjoy food and drinks together. The richest homes have more expensive furniture and decorate tables with tablecloths, and the chairs with fabric padding.
sitting-areas.name: Sitting area

soaps.description: Hand washing with soap reduces the risk of diarrhoeal disease, a leading cause of child mortality. The poorest families usually have a bar of soap to wash their hands with. Families with a higher income tend to buy soap in branded packages and keep it in a clean bucket or plastic box. The richest families buy liquid soap dispensers for hand washing, choosing from many fragrances and colours.
soaps.name: Soap for hands and body

social-drinks.description: Drinks that families enjoy together vary more across income level than they do location. The poorest families prize clean water highly, and those with some spare money heat it up with tea or coffee. Wealthier families buy juice, alcoholic and fizzy drinks. The richest homes buy manufactured tea bags and coffee machines for convenience, a luxury poorer homes cannot afford.
social-drinks.name: Social drink

steam-exits.description: A chimney or steam exit prevents household air pollution. For the poorest, solid fuels like animal dung or charcoal are often burnt for cooking and heating. These fuels produce hazardous fumes like carbon monoxide. To prevent the buildup of smoke over stoves, the poorest have gaps in the roofing, while wealthier homes have purpose-made ventilation. The richest use electronic steam extractors over their stoves.
steam-exits.name: Smoke and steam exit

stoves.description: A family’s stove type depends on income and access to clean fuels. The poorest, who are often in rural areas, use open charcoal or animal dung fires to heat a traditional or side-feed stove. Those with higher incomes use clean burning fuels like gas or electricity. The richest homes have integrated stoves and ovens that are safe, fan powered and have ready access to fuel.
stoves.name: Stove/hob

tables-with-food.description: The poorest survive on just one or two staple ingredients and availability varies according to season. They spend most of their income on food. Those with more money can eat food according to preference, nutritious value and taste, making meals using all food groups like dairy products, fruits and vegetables. The richest families can eat food imported from all over the world.
tables-with-food.name: Table with food

things-i-dream-of-having.description: The poorest families dream of getting out of poverty and having a bicycle, piece of land or a better house. Families who do not live under the poverty line dream of affluence and education. Middle income families wish for a university education and having a big house. The richest families dream of flying to new places and buying cars.
things-i-dream-of-having.name: Thing I dream about having

toilet-paper.description: The poorest families use water or leaves to clean themselves after the toilet. With more money families might start using toilet paper. The richest families use a roll of toilet paper. They also have a special brush and washing liquid to clean the toilet with.
toilet-paper.name: Toilet paper

toilets.description: The poorest families, particularly in rural areas, practice open defecation or use shallow pit latrines. Families with a higher income, especially in cities, have more access to improved sanitation facilities. Many middle income homes use ventilated outhouses with deep pits, protecting food and water sources from contamination. The richest families use integrated squat or seating toilets with a flush or septic tank to safely separate human excreta from human contact.
toilets.name: Toilet

toothbrushes.description: The poorest homes do not have toothbrushes, but use twigs and sand as toothpick tools instead. Families with a slightly higher income buy a plastic toothbrush to share since they cannot afford one each. The richest homes often buy special teeth cleaning products like flavored toothpaste, mouthwash or an electric toothbrush.
toothbrushes.name: Toothbrush

toys.description: Playing is important for early childhood development. The poorest families are not able to buy manufactured toys. Instead, children play with discarded objects in and outside the home. Wealthier families all over the world buy and make toys for their children, like footballs, wooden animals and teddy bears. The richest children also play with high-tech electronic games.
toys.name: Toys

turning-fan-ac-on.description: Turning on the source of cool
turning-fan-ac-on.name: Turning fan/ac on

vegetables.description: Vegetable consumption is important to prevent against chronic disease. Low income families eat locally grown produce, and usually just have a couple to choose from at any one time. Those with more money can choose their preferred type from markets and shops. The richest eat their favourite vegetables imported from all over the world and store them in their fridge or in purpose made vegetable containers.
vegetables.name: Vegetables

washing-clothes.description: The poorest usually wash their clothes in open water or a bucket, without specialised washing liquid. Middle income families often have a tap supplying running water. The richest families use washing, and sometimes drying, machines to clean their clothes.
washing-clothes.name: Washing clothes/cleaning

what-i-wish-i-could-buy.name: What I wish I could buy
what-i-wish-i-could-buy.name_plural: What I wish I could buy

work-areas.description: The poorest families work areas all look different and are often outside, since they often do physical work like rickshaw driving, sewing or farming. Those with a higher income sometimes install a desk to work or study at along with a comfortable chair. The richest homes have more disposable income to spend on work areas with desk lamps, computers and printing equipment.
work-areas.name: Work area

beds.description: Materials, positioning and style of beds change across income levels. The poorest make do with natural fibres and unclean surfaces, while homes with more money sleep on raised platforms with purpose-made bedding for comfort. The richest homes often have more or less the same style mattresses, duvets and pillows, suggesting that there is globalized version of a comfortable night’s sleep.
beds.name: Bed

families.description: Families all over the World are more similar than we might think. The poorest still get many children, but most families have about two children. Sometimes families take care of their elderly relatives as well as their children.
families.name: Family

floors.description: Those with the lowest income, especially in rural areas, make do with dirt or sand flooring which is hard to keep clean. Those with a higher income tend to have a tiled or plastic lino floor that is cheap to install and easy to maintain. The richest homes invest in ceramic or stone tiles and wooden floorboards to suit their preference.

place.name: Family 266
place.aboutData: In this household each adult can consume goods and services worth about 685 US dollars each month. This consumption includes the things they buy as well as the things they produce for themselves (if any). We estimated this figure based on incomes reported by the family.
place.description:
The  family lives in Brazil. K is 24 years old and she works in telemarketing. Her brother M is 22 years old and he has a skilled job in production.

The family lives in their own 3 bedroom house and has been living here for 3 years. They like the size and location of the house. However, they dislike its lack of security. The house has uninterrupted electricity, indoors toilet facility, and safe supply of water.

The Family buys all of their food supplies from the market and spends around 30% of their income on it. They cook their food on LPG fuel. Drinking water is also available at their home and is safe to drink.

The family has been on vacations and has traveled as far as Vitoria, Brazil. Their favorite items in the house are the documents, mobile phones, TV, guitar etc. They are saving money and their next big plan is to buy a new TV and some living room furniture. Their dream is to buy a car.

Their next big plan is to buy a TV and living room furniture. Their dream is to buy a car.

books.description: Families living on a very low income sometimes have poor literacy skills and often do not keep many books. Middle income families often have a big collection of children’s picture books and textbooks, which boosts children’s literacy rates. The richest families often borrow books from the library or buy novels to read for pleasure and so have a whole shelving unit allocated for books.
books.name: Books

computers.description: The poorest homes cannot afford computers or internet connections. Those with a higher income often have an affordable laptop or desktop connected to the internet through a cable. They might also use a smartphone connected to 3G data.  The richest homes often have high-tech computers complete with printing equipment and broadband internet.
computers.name: Computer

cooking-utensils.description: The cooking utensils a family has depends on economic level more than geographic region. The poorest families usually have one or two wooden spoons, metal serving spoons or sharp knives. Wealthier families have more materials to choose from, like colourful and heatproof plastics and stainless steel. The richest families have purpose made containers to display and organise their stash of various cooking utensils.
cooking-utensils.name: Cooking utensils

cups.description: Cups are functional and hold liquids that we drink, but also have a social use. The poorest around the world have just a small selection for drinking both hot and cold drinks. Those with a bit more money have special ceramic cups for hot and glass or metal cups for cold drinks. The richest families have diverse shapes, colours and materials on display in their kitchen cupboards or shelves.
cups.name: Cups/mugs/glasses

dish-brushes.description: The poorest families use rags made out of natural fibres or sometimes grit to wash plates. They do not tend to have manufactured materials or washing liquid. Those with more money use scrubbing brushes made of metal or plastic. The richest families use specially designed and colourful instruments to scrub plates clean. They have purpose made sinks or dishwasher machines.
dish-brushes.name: Dish washing brush/cloth

dish-racks.description: The poorest homes dry their small selection of metal or plastic dishes in a bowl or on the floor. Homes with a high income have a larger selection made out of different materials and leave dishes to dry in a purpose made drying space with bars allowing water to drain through. The richest homes sometimes have dishwashers.
dish-racks.name: Dish racks

families.description: Families all over the World are more similar than we might think. The poorest still get many children, but most families have about two children. Sometimes families take care of their elderly relatives as well as their children.
families.name: Family

Those with a higher income tend to have a tiled or plastic lino floor that is cheap to install and easy to maintain. The richest homes invest in ceramic or stone tiles and wooden floorboards to suit their preference.
floors.name: Floor

fruits.description: Fruit consumption is important to prevent chronic disease. Low income families can afford to eat only locally grown fruit when in season. Those with more money can also choose their preferred fruit from markets and shops. The richest can eat fruit imported from all over the world and store it in special fruit bowls or in their fridge.
fruits.name: Fruits and vegetables

get-water.description: Families living in rural poor communities often have to walk to water sources, and might lack clean drinking water. Middle income families tend to have improved water sources from taps which they might share with other families. They also tend to have a septic tank or filtering mechanism ensuring the water is clean. The richest homes have taps with reliable drinking water integrated into kitchens and bathrooms.
get-water.name: Get water

hand-washing.description: Hand washing after using the toilet is important for every family’s health. To do this, the poorest families collect water from wells or communal taps in plastic buckets or metal pots. Those with more money install an outdoor tap which can be used for hand washing. The richest have sinks with hot and cold taps installed inside their home which is easily accessible from the toilet.
hand-washing.name: Hand washing

jewelry.description: Jewelry can be a life-saving insurance policy because it can be quickly exchanged for cash in a medical emergency. The poorest cannot afford any jewelry of value. For those with a higher income, jewelry is made from different materials like glass beads, gold and silver and is worn for pleasure. The richest often have jewelry boxes in their homes where they store many colorful necklaces, rings and earrings.
jewelry.name: Jewelry

The richest families have purpose made containers to display and organise their stash of various cooking utensils.

The richest families have diverse shapes, colours and materials on display in their kitchen cupboards or shelves.

The richest homes sometimes have dishwashers.
dish-racks.name: Dish racks

fruits.name: Fruits and vegetables

get-water.name: Get water

The richest have sinks with hot and cold taps installed inside their home which is easily accessible from the toilet.
hand-washing.name: Hand washing

how-the-most-loved-item-is-used.name: How the most loved item is used

jewelry.description: Jewelry can be a life-saving insurance policy because it can be quickly exchanged for cash in a medical emergency. The poorest cannot afford any jewelry of value. The richest families keep many painkillers, preventative medicines and vitamin pills in cupboards or on shelves.
medication.name: Medication

next-big-things-i-plan-to-buy.name: Next big thing you are planning to buy

nicest-shoes.name: Nicest shoes

Those with a higher income sometimes have ring bound notebooks or diaries to keep notes and dates in. The richest families also keep packs of white paper in their home for printing.
papers.name: Paper

pens.description: Not all low income families have pens at home, since they might not read and write regularly. The richest families can buy all types of mass-manufactured pens and so usually have a large collection at home.
pens.name: Pen/pencils

The richest families have a lot of different condiments to choose from and salt is placed in a designated space in the family’s kitchen.
salt.name: Salt

shaving.name: Shaving

The richest families buy liquid soap dispensers for hand washing, choosing from many fragrances and colours.
