place.aboutData: In this household each adult can consume goods and services worth about 685 US dollars each month. This consumption includes the things they buy as well as the things they produce for themselves (if any). We estimated this figure based on incomes reported by the family.
place.description:
The  family lives in Brazil. K is 24 years old and she works in telemarketing. Her brother M is 22 years old and he has a skilled job in production.

The family lives in their own 3 bedroom house and has been living here for 3 years. They like the size and location of the house. However, they dislike its lack of security. The house has uninterrupted electricity, indoors toilet facility, and safe supply of water.

The Family buys all of their food supplies from the market and spends around 30% of their income on it. They cook their food on LPG fuel. Drinking water is also available at their home and is safe to drink.

The family has been on vacations and has traveled as far as Vitoria, Brazil. Their favorite items in the house are the documents, mobile phones, TV, guitar etc. They are saving money and their next big plan is to buy a new TV and some living room furniture. Their dream is to buy a car.

soaps.description: Hand washing with soap reduces the risk of diarrhoeal disease, a leading cause of child mortality. The poorest families usually have a bar of soap to wash their hands with. Families with a higher income tend to buy soap in branded packages and keep it in a clean bucket or plastic box. The richest families buy liquid soap dispensers for hand washing, choosing from many fragrances and colours.
soaps.name: Soap for hands and body

social-drinks.description: Drinks that families enjoy together vary more across income level than they do location. The poorest families prize clean water highly, and those with some spare money heat it up with tea or coffee. Wealthier families buy juice, alcoholic and fizzy drinks. The richest homes buy manufactured tea bags and coffee machines for convenience, a luxury poorer homes cannot afford.
social-drinks.name: Social drink

steam-exits.description: A chimney or steam exit prevents household air pollution. For the poorest, solid fuels like animal dung or charcoal are often burnt for cooking and heating. These fuels produce hazardous fumes like carbon monoxide. To prevent the buildup of smoke over stoves, the poorest have gaps in the roofing, while wealthier homes have purpose-made ventilation. The richest use electronic steam extractors over their stoves.
steam-exits.name: Smoke and steam exit

stoves.description: A family’s stove type depends on income and access to clean fuels. The poorest, who are often in rural areas, use open charcoal or animal dung fires to heat a traditional or side-feed stove. Those with higher incomes use clean burning fuels like gas or electricity. The richest homes have integrated stoves and ovens that are safe, fan powered and have ready access to fuel.
stoves.name: Stove/hob

tables-with-food.description: The poorest survive on just one or two staple ingredients and availability varies according to season. They spend most of their income on food. Those with more money can eat food according to preference, nutritious value and taste, making meals using all food groups like dairy products, fruits and vegetables. The richest families can eat food imported from all over the world.
tables-with-food.name: Table with food

things-i-dream-of-having.description: The poorest families dream of getting out of poverty and having a bicycle, piece of land or a better house. Families who do not live under the poverty line dream of affluence and education. Middle income families wish for a university education and having a big house. The richest families dream of flying to new places and buying cars.
things-i-dream-of-having.name: Thing I dream about having

toilet-paper.description: The poorest families use water or leaves to clean themselves after the toilet. With more money families might start using toilet paper. The richest families use a roll of toilet paper. They also have a special brush and washing liquid to clean the toilet with.
toilet-paper.name: Toilet paper

toilets.description: The poorest families, particularly in rural areas, practice open defecation or use shallow pit latrines. Families with a higher income, especially in cities, have more access to improved sanitation facilities. Many middle income homes use ventilated outhouses with deep pits, protecting food and water sources from contamination. The richest families use integrated squat or seating toilets with a flush or septic tank to safely separate human excreta from human contact.
toilets.name: Toilet

toothbrushes.description: The poorest homes do not have toothbrushes, but use twigs and sand as toothpick tools instead. Families with a slightly higher income buy a plastic toothbrush to share since they cannot afford one each. The richest homes often buy special teeth cleaning products like flavored toothpaste, mouthwash or an electric toothbrush.
toothbrushes.name: Toothbrush

toys.description: Playing is important for early childhood development. The poorest families are not able to buy manufactured toys. Instead, children play with discarded objects in and outside the home. Wealthier families all over the world buy and make toys for their children, like footballs, wooden animals and teddy bears. The richest children also play with high-tech electronic games.
toys.name: Toys

turning-fan-ac-on.description: Turning on the source of cool
turning-fan-ac-on.name: Turning fan/ac on

vegetables.description: Vegetable consumption is important to prevent against chronic disease. Low income families eat locally grown produce, and usually just have a couple to choose from at any one time. Those with more money can choose their preferred type from markets and shops. The richest eat their favourite vegetables imported from all over the world and store them in their fridge or in purpose made vegetable containers.
vegetables.name: Vegetables

washing-clothes.description: The poorest usually wash their clothes in open water or a bucket, without specialised washing liquid. Middle income families often have a tap supplying running water. The richest families use washing, and sometimes drying, machines to clean their clothes.
washing-clothes.name: Washing clothes/cleaning

what-i-wish-i-could-buy.name: What I wish I could buy
what-i-wish-i-could-buy.name_plural: What I wish I could buy

work-areas.description: The poorest families work areas all look different and are often outside, since they often do physical work like rickshaw driving, sewing or farming. Those with a higher income sometimes install a desk to work or study at along with a comfortable chair. The richest homes have more disposable income to spend on work areas with desk lamps, computers and printing equipment.
work-areas.name: Work area

beds.description: Materials, positioning and style of beds change across income levels. The poorest make do with natural fibres and unclean surfaces, while homes with more money sleep on raised platforms with purpose-made bedding for comfort. The richest homes often have more or less the same style mattresses, duvets and pillows, suggesting that there is globalized version of a comfortable night’s sleep.
beds.name: Bed

families.description: Families all over the World are more similar than we might think. The poorest still get many children, but most families have about two children. Sometimes families take care of their elderly relatives as well as their children.
families.name: Family

floors.description: Those with the lowest income, especially in rural areas, make do with dirt or sand flooring which is hard to keep clean. Those with a higher income tend to have a tiled or plastic lino floor that is cheap to install and easy to maintain. The richest homes invest in ceramic or stone tiles and wooden floorboards to suit their preference.
